transcripts.onepager_promise: Recommend targeted equipment and process improvements to improve output quality and cycle times
transcripts.prompt: Give me the practical options to improve throughput without hiding the quality tradeoffs.
transcripts.assistant_response:
Here's the throughput picture across all four lines, each with a real quality angle:

**Line 3** (gap 20 uph): cycle-time cut on SMT Station 3B is cheapest (+12 uph, process/tooling only), parallel station adds +17 uph but costs $45K–$120K, quality fix on the same station only buys +4 uph — tradeoff: cycle-time cuts push the bottleneck harder, which is exactly where the 0.1% defect already lives, so squeezing speed without the quality fix risks defect rate creeping up.

**Line A** (gap 38 uph): same pattern — Functional Test cycle-time cut (+23) or parallel unit (+32, $45K–$120K). The real defect risk is downstream at Final Assembly (0.18%), not at the station you'd be speeding up, so there's less direct tension here.

**Line B** (gap 39 uph): Robotic Welding is both the bottleneck and the defect hotspot (0.3%, highest of the four). Cycle-time cut or parallel station speeds up the exact process generating defects — this is the one where "faster" and "lower quality" are most likely to collide.

**Line C** (gap 72 uph, biggest gap): Injection Molding cuts give the largest raw gains (+43 to +61 uph) but it's also running the highest defect rate (0.45%). Chasing throughput here without the quality option risks the worst scrap/rework blowback of the four lines.

Bottom line: parallel-station options buy the most uph but cost real money ($45K–$120K) and don't fix defects; cycle-time cuts are cheaper but stress the bottleneck station, which is often also the defect source — worst on Line B and Line C. Want the full financial/ROI breakdown for any one line?
